title: Is there enough evidence to ban smartphones in schools?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou takes the Haidt debate on smartphones and teen mental health and asks what schools should do when experts disagree and conclusive evidence is absent. Using her time as research director at Ark, she argues that research should be a broad framework for judgement, not a replacement for it, citing Weinberg's chicken soup versus king's touch example on prior plausibility. For school phone bans she shifts the question from mental health to learning, since phones are a distraction and attention is central in multimedia learning research. She also notes the burden of proof was reversed when screens entered schools without robust evidence. Reports from John Wallis Academy on falling detentions and truancy, and even sceptics of the mental-health link agreeing phones do not belong in lessons, lead her to ask who is making the positive case for phones in school.
points: Schools cannot wait for gold-standard trials; evidence should frame judgement rather than replace common sense.
The case for school phone bans rests on learning and attention, not on the contested mental-health claims.
Devices entered classrooms with little evidence, so the burden of proof was framed backwards.
John Wallis Academy reported detentions down 40 per cent and truancy down 25 per cent after introducing a Yondr-based ban.
Even critics of Haidt's mental-health evidence accept that phones should be kept out of lessons, leaving few advocates for the opposing position.
quotes: However, there are plenty of people who disagree with Haidt’s analysis, for a variety of reasons. Some say that actually, there is no teen mental health crisis: it’s all a function of reduced stigma and diagnostic inflation. Others say that there is a mental health crisis, but it’s better explained by other factors, like economic insecurity. Still others argue there is no link between phones & mental health, while others say that there might be a link, but that doesn’t prove that smartphones cause mental health problems.

What are heads and teachers supposed to do when the evidence is unclear or conflicting? To what extent can every decision they make be research informed? Is it the job of teachers to be full time researchers? Surely there always has to be a role for common sense – for making quick judgement calls based on the available evidence rather than spinning your wheels and taking weeks to discover that on the issue you’re interested in, there isn’t really any conclusive evidence one way or the other?

You can never eliminate human judgement. All that we can hope to do, as educators and humans, is to use evidence and research as a broad framework for the many judgements we will have to make that will never have precise gold-standard RCTs informing them.

Phones are a distraction, and distractions aren’t good for learning. The best book I’ve read about the relationship between technology and learning is The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, edited by Richard Mayer. Large chunks of the book are about the importance of attention, and how easily poorly designed multimedia resources can distract attention or focus it on the wrong thing.

Now there is some push back about phones in particular, but the debate has been framed in such a way that we need a series of replicable high-quality randomised controlled trials to prove they are a problem. But the argument could have been framed very differently. We could have said that we wouldn’t introduce any screens into classrooms until we had robust evidence that they improved learning - and if we’d done that, things would now look very different.

Within three or four weeks, “we saw real changes”, McBeath says. Teachers had to change teaching style, to pick up the pace of increased focus. In just one term, detentions have decreased by 40 per cent. The number of students truanting from lessons fell by 25 per cent.
I can’t find anyone making this case. And if there isn’t much of a case, then why aren’t more schools implementing similar policies?
